title: ORNL, IBM, and AMD launch co-design platform for quantum error correction
content: Quantum Research Blog ORNL, IBM, and AMD launch co-design platform for quantum error correction The U.S. DOE’s Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory is leading the integration of the best IBM quantum hardware with ORNL’s powerful compute clusters, powered by AMD. Date 5 Nov 2026 Authors Rafi Letzter Topics Network Community Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key Takeaways: The U.S. Department of Energy’s Quantum Science Center (QSC) at Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and AMD deployed a co-design platform for quantum error correction (QEC) at IBM's site in Poughkeepsie, New York. The QEC co-design platform pairs IBM Quantum Nighthawk r2 processors with ORNL’s Umbra High-Performance Computing (HPC) system, comprising AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen AMD EPYC™ CPUs. Researchers can use the platform to develop and validate quantum algorithms, workflows, and applications for hybrid HPC-quantum computing environments without building the infrastructure themselves. Quantum error correction depends on decoders, the classical software that identifies qubit errors and must keep pace with the quantum processor. Placing ORNL’s hardware next to the IBM quantum processors gives the system low-latency quantum-classical execution. Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and AMD have launched a co-design platform for quantum error correction to help researchers define and accelerate the classical and quantum workflows for scientifically relevant quantum computing. The quantum error correction (QEC) co-design platform sits at IBM's site in Poughkeepsie, New York and launched with the U.S. Department of Energy’s Quantum Science Center (QSC) at ORNL and AMD as its inaugural partners. It pairs IBM Quantum Nighthawk processors with Umbra, QSC’s high-performance computing system comprising AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen AMD EPYC™ CPUs, in one co-located environment linked to ORNL's broader supercomputing ecosystem. This initiative brings together the computing infrastructure needed for quantum error correction in a single environment and opens it up to more researchers than ever before. They will use it to develop and validate quantum algorithms, workflows, and applications in an environment designed for quantum-centric supercomputing, an emerging paradigm where quantum processors, CPUs, and GPUs work together as one system. The platform handles the infrastructure, so researchers can concentrate on algorithm discovery. Loading A co-design platform for quantum error correction This platform builds on IBM and AMD's existing collaboration, including using AMD GPUs to accelerate sample-based quantum diagonalization and demonstrating efficient quantum error decoding on AMD hardware. The collaboration will also explore how future generations of AMD compute, networking and open software can be co-designed with quantum computers. How the co-design platform will advance quantum computing research Qubits, the fundamental units of quantum computation, make errors. Quantum error correction protects against them. Error correcting codes spread information across many qubits and run repeated checks for signs of trouble. A classical computer reads the data from each round of checks and works out which errors occurred. Researchers call the software that does this job a decoder, and it has to keep up with the quantum processor. That’s a fast-paced, demanding, computationally-intensive task. The algorithms that will make quantum computing scientifically useful need substantial classical computing resources working in step with quantum processors. Today, quantum computers and high performance computing (HPC) infrastructure rarely sit in the same location or get directly integrated. That means that researchers working on hybrid workflows often stitch those pieces together themselves. They reach a quantum computer through the cloud, run classical work on separate systems, and connect the two through separate application programming interfaces (APIs), the software links that let one system talk to another. Every handoff adds complexity and delay, and limits the experiments researchers can run. Error correction lays the foundation for practically relevant quantum computing. Its value comes from what it unlocks: larger, deeper, more capable quantum computations. The QEC co-design platform lets researchers test error correction on real quantum systems, inside the workflows it will serve. It also enables researchers to explore the use of GPUs for low-latency decoding more broadly. One promising approach is hierarchical error correction, and the platform could support research in that direction. The hierarchical approach layers two codes. An inner code protects qubits within a module. An outer code wraps around the inner code’s logical qubits and adds a second layer of protection.
